```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Spatial proximity is not always a straight-line distance. Observations might
represent adjacent districts, locations separated by a peninsula, or points
on the globe. The appropriate smooth depends on that geometry. This article
uses three examples to show how to fit those models and interpret gratia's
effect displays.

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library("mgcv")
library("gratia")
library("ggplot2")
```

The examples require mgcv 1.9-4 or later. Spherical plotting also needs the
optional sf package. Three-dimensional views need ggcube. The district and
soap-film analyses run without either optional display package.

## Are high crime rates explained by district income or location?

The Columbus data supplied with mgcv record residential burglary and auto
theft rates per 1,000 households in 49 districts. They also record household
income in thousands of dollars and provide district polygons. These are
**rates**, not counts, so fitting a Poisson distribution to `crime` would
misrepresent the response. A Gaussian model is a starting approximation for
variation in rates; a count model would require counts and exposure data.
See the [data documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/mgcv/html/columb.html)
for the original source.

We adapt the worked examples in mgcv's
[Markov random field documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/mgcv/html/smooth.construct.mrf.smooth.spec.html).
The smooth gives each district an effect and penalises differences between
neighbours. Neighbourhoods are derived from polygons that share vertices.

```{r columbus-data}
data("columb", package = "mgcv")
data("columb.polys", package = "mgcv")
ggplot(columb, aes(income, crime)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Household income (thousands of dollars)",
    y = "Burglaries and auto thefts per 1,000 households")
```

Start with the spatial pattern alone, and compare a full representation with a
smaller one before adding income:

```{r columbus-models}
district_full <- gam(crime ~ s(district, bs = "mrf",
  xt = list(polys = columb.polys)), data = columb, method = "REML")
district_small <- gam(crime ~ s(district, bs = "mrf", k = 20,
  xt = list(polys = columb.polys)), data = columb, method = "REML")
district_income <- gam(crime ~ s(district, bs = "mrf", k = 20,
  xt = list(polys = columb.polys)) + s(income, k = 6),
  data = columb, method = "REML")
overview(district_income)
```

The full model has a district coefficient for every area, subject to centring
and the estimated penalty. The reduced representation uses fewer coefficients
to represent the same 49 area effects. `k = 20` restricts the available spatial
patterns; it does not mean only twenty districts are fitted. Adding income
asks how much spatial variation remains after accounting for its association
with crime rate.

## Read district effects rather than basis coefficients

```{r district-estimates}
area_effects <- smooth_estimates(district_income, select = "s(district)",
  interval = "credible")
head(area_effects)
```

The rows are effects for **areas**, even for a reduced-rank fit. They are not
the coefficients of its smaller basis. The same area labels identify
predictions supplied with `data`; a previously unknown district is not a
valid prediction location merely because it is adjacent to one in the model.

```{r district-effects, fig.height = 6}
draw(area_effects, angle = 90,
  ylab = "District contribution to crime rate", xlab = "District")
draw(district_income, select = "s(income)",
  xlab = "Household income (thousands of dollars)",
  ylab = "Income contribution to crime rate")
```

Positive area effects indicate rates above the fitted intercept and income
contribution. The income association is downward over this dataset's range,
while individual adjusted district effects have substantial uncertainty. Use
their intervals when comparing districts. Neighbouring districts borrow
information through the penalty on the mean effects. The Gaussian response
errors are still assumed independent, so inspect residual spatial patterns
before relying on these intervals.

To see how much the smaller spatial representation changes the fitted pattern,
compare its area effects on the same district labels:

```{r district-rank-comparison}
rank_effects <- rbind(
  transform(smooth_estimates(district_full), representation = "Full"),
  transform(smooth_estimates(district_small), representation = "Reduced")
)
ggplot(rank_effects, aes(district, .estimate, colour = representation)) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "District", y = "District contribution to crime rate",
    colour = "Representation") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1))
```

The comparison shows how reducing the basis changes the spatial-only fits.
Use it to assess whether the smaller representation retains the district
patterns of interest. The neighbourhood graph determines which area effects
borrow information from each other, so check that it represents the
connections relevant to your analysis.

```{r district-qq}
draw(district_income, select = "s(district)", mrf_plot = "qq")
```

This QQ view describes the distribution of fitted area effects. They are
correlated and can have unequal marginal variances, so this is not a test of
independent normal effects or a response-distribution diagnostic. For response
checks use `appraise()` and consult
[Choosing diagnostic references](model-checking.html).

One can also inspect the neighbourhood penalty itself:

```{r district-penalty, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6}
draw(penalty(district_income, select = "s(district)"), geom = "tile")
```

This is the penalty expressed in the fitted reduced basis; its rows are
basis coefficients rather than districts. Larger diagonal entries indicate
coefficient directions that are penalised more strongly. Before its basis
transformation, the MRF penalty counts neighbours on the diagonal and uses
negative off-diagonal entries for neighbours. Use the area plots above to
inspect district labels and intervals; the penalty plot explains how their
underlying coefficients are regularised.

## How should a surface behave across a peninsula?

For a bounded region such as a water body, locations on opposite sides of land
can be close in Euclidean distance and distant along the water. A soap-film
smooth respects the supplied boundary. We use a simulation from mgcv's
[soap-film example](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/mgcv/html/smooth.construct.so.smooth.spec.html),
retaining its curved boundary, interior knots and simulated test surface. The
question is whether a boundary-aware smoother can recover a field without joining
opposite sides across the excluded region. We use REML instead of the
example's default smoothing selection.

```{r soap-data}
bnd <- list(mgcv::fs.boundary())
names(bnd[[1]]) <- c("v", "w")
interior_knots <- expand.grid(v = seq(-0.5, 3, by = 0.5),
  w = c(-0.6, -0.3, 0.3, 0.6))
set.seed(0)
v <- runif(600, -1, 4)
w <- runif(600, -1, 1)
truth <- mgcv::fs.test(v, w, b = 1)
y <- truth + rnorm(600, sd = 0.3)
inside <- mgcv::inSide(bnd, x = v, y = w)
water <- data.frame(v = v[inside], w = w[inside],
  y = y[inside], truth = truth[inside])
ggplot(water, aes(v, w, colour = y)) +
  geom_path(data = as.data.frame(bnd[[1]]), aes(v, w),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "v coordinate", y = "w coordinate", colour = "Observed field")
```

The errors were generated as independent Gaussian noise with standard
deviation 0.3, matching the Gaussian identity-link model fitted below.

## Separate boundary variation from interior variation

```{r soap-component-fit}
water_fit <- gam(y ~
    s(v, w, bs = "sf", k = 30, xt = list(bnd = bnd, nmax = 100)) +
    s(v, w, bs = "sw", k = 30, xt = list(bnd = bnd, nmax = 100)),
  data = water, knots = interior_knots, method = "REML")
overview(water_fit)
smooths(water_fit)
```

`sf` estimates a cyclic smooth around the closed boundary and extends it
into the interior as a surface satisfying Laplace's equation. The first panel
shows that surface, rather than just the values along the boundary. `sw`
adds interior variation that is zero on the boundary. Both components are
estimated jointly; their sum plus the intercept gives the complete fitted
mean. The boundary basis size is `k`; the interior basis size comes from the number of supplied knots.
`nmax = 100` sets the numerical solution grid, rather than the plotting grid.
Both component types now have distinct labels in gratia.

Both terms happen to have the same `s(v,w)` label. Select them by numerical
position when you need one component rather than both:

```{r soap-components, fig.height = 6}
draw(water_fit, n_2d = 35, surface = "tile", caption = TRUE, ncol = 1,
  scales = "fixed", contour = FALSE,
  xlab = "v coordinate", ylab = "w coordinate")
```

In this simulation REML shrinks the interior adjustment almost to zero,
so the second panel is nearly flat on the shared colour scale. The surface
induced by the boundary accounts for almost all the fitted variation. Effect colours
display each centred contribution; add them and the intercept to recover
the fitted mean field.
Boundary loops remain visible and predictions outside the supplied domain
are unavailable.

```{r soap-saved-estimates}
interior_effect <- smooth_estimates(water_fit, select = 2,
  n_2d = 30, clip = TRUE)
head(interior_effect)
```

`clip = TRUE` removes evaluation cells outside the boundary. Without clipping,
those locations retain missing estimates. Boundary rows are retained as
plotting information and are identified by `.bndry`; they are not additional
observations. Saved estimates retain the component identity so `draw()` can
reproduce its boundary-aware display.

The simulated truth makes it possible to assess the complete fitted surface:

```{r soap-recovery}
water$estimated <- fitted(water_fit)
sqrt(mean((water$estimated - water$truth)^2))
ggplot(water, aes(truth, estimated)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Simulated mean field", y = "Estimated mean field")
```

The fitted values follow the simulated mean closely at the sampled locations.
When adapting this model to a water body, place interior knots across the
domain and include boundary features that must prevent smoothing across land.
sf/sw components can also form space-by-time tensor products; the flat-surface display uses numeric
conditioning slices for time. Transformed soap-film boundaries currently
cannot be drawn on a recovered raw covariate scale: retain the model-scale
display rather than silently dropping the boundary.

## How do we avoid a seam at the date line?

A plane is a poor representation for a global surface: points immediately
either side of the date line are neighbours, and all longitudes meet at a
pole. A spline on the sphere uses that geometry. We adapt mgcv's
[spherical smooth example](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/mgcv/html/smooth.construct.sos.smooth.spec.html)
as a synthetic sensor survey. Sampling latitude through `asin()` gives uniform
area density directly. We remove the example's latitude shift in the test
function so the simulated field is continuous at both poles, and use REML.
The units are arbitrary; this is a controlled field-recovery exercise.

```{r sphere-data-fit}
set.seed(90)
globe <- data.frame(
  latitude = asin(runif(400, -1, 1)) * 180 / pi,
  longitude = runif(400, -180, 180)
)
globe$truth <- with(globe,
  sin(longitude * pi / 180) * cos(latitude * pi / 180))
globe$observed <- globe$truth + rnorm(400, sd = 0.2)
globe_fit <- gam(observed ~ s(latitude, longitude, bs = "sos", k = 60),
  data = globe, method = "REML")
sqrt(mean((fitted(globe_fit) - globe$truth)^2))
```

The smooth requires latitude first and longitude second, in degrees. A
Gaussian fit matches the generated observation errors. The recovery error
summarises the difference between the fitted and simulated mean at the sampled
locations.

```{r sphere-map, fig.height = 6}
if (requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)) {
  draw(globe_fit, n_2d = 35, rug = TRUE,
    crs = "+proj=ortho +lat_0=20 +lon_0=0")
}
```

The orthographic view shows one hemisphere. Surface cells, contours and
observation points are clipped to that visible hemisphere before projection,
so locations on the far side cannot leak into the display. Cells at poles and
the date line retain valid geographic boundaries. Changing the projection
changes which locations are visible while retaining the fitted spherical
surface. Factor-by spherical effects use separate panels for each level.
Supply a regular prediction grid for a cell map; a scattered prediction
dataset is drawn as points.

Choose the geometry from the question: district neighbourhoods for aggregated
area measurements, soap films for a bounded continuous domain, and spherical
splines for global locations. The boundary and projection controls then let
the displayed surface follow the geometry used in fitting.
